title: The Wooden Barrack to the Ilyin School: Traditionalism, Eurasia, and the Bomb on the Mozhayskoye Highway
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Wooden Barrack on Yuzhinsky Pereulok

stops.name: Moscow, born to an officer of military intelligence
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date and city are confirmed twice over by hostile documents, the US OFAC designation record and the EU Official Journal L259I (2022) entry, both giving 7 January 1962, Moscow. No hospital, district, or address is documented anywhere; the pin is city centre.
stops.campa: Aleksandr Gelyevich Dugin is born in Moscow to Geliy Aleksandrovich Dugin, an officer of Soviet military intelligence, and Galina Viktorovna Onufrienko, a physician. The parents separate when the boy is three. He grows up inside the Soviet service class, in its apartments and its silences, and he will spend his adult life arguing that the state which produced him was fighting the right enemy for entirely the wrong reasons. His father's service is named in his own account only as probably the GRU.
suggested_refs: The OFAC and EU sanctions entries, which agree with each other on his birth date and with nothing else about him

stops.name: Moscow Aviation Institute, two years and an expulsion nobody agrees on
stops.date_confidence: entry in 1979 attested; the departure and its cause are disputed. Russian Wikipedia says he left after the second year, which puts it in 1981. Three incompatible accounts circulate: expelled for anti-Soviet activity and forbidden literature, failed academically, or graduated after all (Dunlop, Stanford FSI: 'According to another account, he eventually managed to graduate'). Not adjudicated. Coordinates from the institute's own infobox, correcting a 1.2 km error in the research pool.
stops.campa: He enters the Moscow Aviation Institute at seventeen, on Volokolamskoye Shosse, where the Soviet Union trains the engineers of its aerospace. He lasts two years. One account has him expelled for anti-Soviet activity and forbidden literature, which is the version the movement prefers; another has him simply failing; a third has him graduating after all. He takes a correspondence degree years later from an engineering and reclamation institute in Novocherkassk, and produces it at his dissertation defence. In the interval, by the standard telling, he sweeps streets.
suggested_refs: The Novocherkassk Engineering-Reclamation Institute correspondence degree, produced at the 2000 defence
sources: John B. Dunlop, 'Aleksandr Dugin's Foundations of Geopolitics', Stanford FSI

stops.name: Yuzhinsky Pereulok, the circle that outlived its founder
stops.date_confidence: the milieu and the reading list are attested (Laruelle OP294, Dunlop, Wikipedia); the year of his entry is reconstruction. Yuzhinsky Pereulok is the 1929-1993 name of Bolshoy Palashyovsky Pereulok; coordinates from ru.wikipedia, correcting a 400 m error. The barrack is gone; the pin is the lane, not a door.
stops.campa: A six-flat wooden barrack stands on Yuzhinsky Pereulok, one flat belonging to the novelist Yuri Mamleev, and the circle that formed there keeps meeting after Mamleev himself has emigrated. The poet and esotericist Evgeny Golovin presides over what is left. Dugin arrives in his late teens with Geydar Dzhemal. The reading is Rene Guenon and Julius Evola on the decline of the modern world, with Nietzsche, Heidegger and a great deal of occultism behind them, and the premise underneath all of it is that the West's whole project is a fall and not a progress. They read at night, in a wooden room, drinking.
suggested_refs: The Yuzhinsky circle of Mamleev, Golovin and Dzhemal, the Soviet Union's principal Traditionalist underground
sources: Marlene Laruelle, ISN ETH Zurich OP294

stops.name: Lenin Library, the forged reader's card
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The anecdote recurs across sympathetic and hostile profiles alike and he has not denied it, but no card, register entry, or borrowing slip has ever been produced. A rival and equally unverified story puts him in a KGB archive instead. Date assigned only to order the segment.
stops.campa: The story the circle tells about him, and that he does not deny, is that he obtains a forged reader's card and works the closed stacks of the Lenin Library on Vozdvizhenka, taking out books a Soviet citizen of no standing has no right to open: Traditionalists, interwar radicals, the whole European counter-Enlightenment. A rival version puts him in a KGB archive instead. The reading is legible in everything he writes for the next forty-five years, whatever room he did it in. No card survives, no register entry, no borrowing slip, and no document says which of the two rooms it was, if either.
suggested_refs: The closed collections (spetskhran) of the Lenin Library, Vozdvizhenka 3/5

stops.name: Moscow, Pagan Imperialism typed into samizdat
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The translation is universally reported as the first act of his intellectual life; the 1981 date rests on movement and scholarly reconstruction rather than on any dated surviving copy. No samizdat artefact was reached. Month assigned only to order the segment.
stops.campa: He translates Julius Evola's Heidnischer Imperialismus, Pagan Imperialism, from the 1933 German edition into Russian, and it goes out in samizdat, typed and retyped by hand and passed between flats. It is the earliest act of his intellectual life anyone can name, and forty-two years later he will publish a book-length study of the same man. Evola himself has been dead seven years by now, in a Rome flat, having asked at the end to be set upright and turned to face the Janiculum.
suggested_refs: Julius Evola, Heidnischer Imperialismus (Leipzig, 1933), the German edition Dugin worked from

stops.name: Moscow, the tapes of Hans Zievers
stops.date_confidence: attested for the range 1981-1984 (Wikipedia), in the Cyrillic transcription Zievers; the research pool's single year of 1982 is not documented. The 1983 date here is a midpoint assigned to order the segment.
stops.campa: Between 1981 and 1984 he records experimental music under a Cyrillic alter ego, Hans Zievers, taken from Wolfram Sievers of the Ahnenerbe, the SS research institute whose director was hanged at Nuremberg for experiments on prisoners. The tapes circulate in the same cellars as the samizdat and among the same few dozen people. It is the underground's habitual provocation, a name chosen for what it will do to a Soviet listener. Some of the recordings still circulate.
suggested_refs: The Hans Zievers tapes, 1981-1984

segments.name: Out of the Cellar: Pamyat and the Officers

stops.name: Moscow, the central council of Pamyat
stops.date_confidence: attested for the membership and the brief council seat; whether he left in 1989 or was expelled is not settled by any source reached. No meeting venue is documented; the pin is city centre.
stops.campa: He joins the National-Patriotic Front Pamyat under Dmitry Vasilyev, bringing Dzhemal with him out of the cellar, and sits briefly on its central council. Pamyat is the first mass Russian nationalist organization of the perestroika years and its politics are ethnic antisemitism and nostalgia for the tsar. It is his first attempt to attach the reading of the barrack to an organization with members, and it lasts about a year. Whether he walked out or was thrown out, the sources contradict each other.
suggested_refs: The National-Patriotic Front Pamyat under Dmitry Vasilyev

stops.name: Brussels, the Dublin to Vladivostok horizon
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, downgraded from the research pool's attested tag. What is documented is only that Dugin's journal Elementy praised Thiriart's Euro-Soviet empire concept. No meeting between the two men is documented and no date is given by any source reached. Thiriart died 23 November 1992, which fixes the outer edge of the window and nothing else. City-level pin.
stops.campa: Jean-Francois Thiriart has spent thirty years arguing for a single European empire running from Dublin to Vladivostok, built against the United States and indifferent to which ideology administers it. Dugin's journal Elementy takes up the Euro-Soviet concept and prints it in praise. Thiriart is old and in Brussels, and the young Russian just out of a Moscow cellar is among the last people in Europe taking his continental empire seriously. It is the map Dugin will keep redrawing. Whether the two men ever met is recorded nowhere; Thiriart dies on 23 November 1992.
suggested_refs: Jean-Francois Thiriart's Euro-Soviet empire, championed in the journal Elementy

stops.name: Moscow, Arktogeia
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1991 by ru.wikipedia, which gives him as chairman of the Arktogeia historical-religious association from that year; the research pool's 1990 and 'c. 1990-1991' are both looser. The Center for Meta-Strategic Studies is reconstruction. No street address for the early office is documented.
stops.campa: He founds Arktogeia, taking the name from the Greek for north and earth, the Hyperborean land at the top of the world that the Traditionalists place at the origin of the Indo-European peoples. It is a publishing house, an association, and a machine for putting Rene Guenon, Julius Evola and the European right into Russian for the first time. Alongside it he sets up a Center for Meta-Strategic Studies and moves close to Alexander Prokhanov, whose weekly Den is where the communists and the nationalists are learning to talk to each other.
suggested_refs: The Arktogeia list, the first Russian-language edition of much of the Traditionalist canon

stops.name: Military Academy of the General Staff, the April roundtable
stops.date_confidence: attested; Dunlop confirms the event verbatim, with every participant by name and rank. Coordinate contradiction flagged and not resolved: the Academy's infobox gives Vernadskogo Prospekt 100 (55.6498, 37.4740), while the same article's body text cites 14 Kholzunova Lane in Khamovniki, about 10 km away. No source specifies which building hosted the roundtable. Day of month assigned to order the segment.
stops.campa: With Prokhanov he organizes a roundtable inside the Military Academy of the General Staff. Alain de Benoist, the principal intellectual of the French Nouvelle Droite, comes from Paris with Jean Lalou. Across the table sit Lieutenant General Nikolai Klokotov, head of the strategy department, his deputy Lieutenant General Nikolai Pishchev, and Major General Vladislav Iminov, head of military history. A man of thirty is explaining the metapolitics of the European New Right to the officers of a vanished army. The state whose general staff this is was dissolved four months ago.
suggested_refs: Dunlop's account of the April 1992 General Staff roundtable, the earliest documented Dugin-de Benoist encounter

stops.name: Moscow, the National Bolshevik Party
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1993 and for the three founders; month assigned to order the segment against the October crisis.
stops.campa: With Eduard Limonov, back from New York and Paris, and the punk singer Yegor Letov, he founds the National Bolshevik Party. Limonov supplies the face, the newspaper Limonka, and the young men willing to be arrested; Dugin supplies the doctrine, the symbols, and the reading list. The thing is built to be unbearable to everyone at once, and for a decade it works. Limonka runs from 1994 to 2002. The party flag sets a hammer and sickle in a white circle on red.
suggested_refs: Limonka, the National Bolshevik newspaper, 1994-2002
sources: RFE/RL on the National Bolshevik Party (rferl.org/a/1058689.html)

stops.name: Russian White House, the tanks on the embankment
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was aligned with the anti-Yeltsin camp; claims of a decisive combat role are explicitly not documented anywhere reached. Coordinates from Wikipedia, 'Russian White House', correcting a 350 m drift in the research pool.
stops.campa: Yeltsin dissolves the parliament; the parliament refuses to be dissolved; for ten days the Supreme Soviet holds the White House on Krasnopresnenskaya Embankment against the president. Dugin is with the opposition, inside the red-brown coalition of communists and nationalists that has formed against Yeltsin and that his own writing helped make thinkable. What he did in those days beyond standing on that side is not established. On the fourth of October the tanks fire from the bridge into the upper floors, in daylight, with the cameras running.
suggested_refs: The October 1993 constitutional crisis and the shelling of the House of Soviets

stops.name: Moscow, nought point eight five percent
stops.date_confidence: the vote share is attested verbatim in Dunlop; the district is not. Dunlop names no constituency, and no source confirming the research pool's St Petersburg attribution was found, so the stop has been relocated from St Petersburg to Moscow as a national and party event. The district remains unknown.
stops.campa: He stands for the State Duma on a National Bolshevik platform and receives 0.85 percent of the vote. The doctrine that is being read in the General Staff and quoted in Washington cannot get one voter in a hundred and twenty. Everything he builds afterward, the publishing house, the movement, the journals, the seminars, the television channel, is built to reach elites over the head of an electorate that has just told him in numbers what it thinks of him. He never stands for anything again.
suggested_refs: The December 1995 State Duma election

stops.name: Moscow, Foundations of Geopolitics
stops.date_confidence: 1997 publication by Arktogeia attested. Authorship contested and left open: Dugin credits Lt Gen Klokotov as co-author and main inspiration, and Klokotov denies it; Colonel General Leonid Ivashov of the Defence Ministry is separately reported to have helped draft it. Month unknown, defaulted. There is no authorized full English translation of the book, so the quotation is a rendering of unknown provenance.
stops.campa: Arktogeia publishes Osnovy geopolitiki, Foundations of Geopolitics, six hundred pages recasting all history as the war of land power against sea power, of Eurasia against the Atlantic. Copies circulate in the General Staff and the military academies and it is put on reading lists. Dugin names Lieutenant General Klokotov as consultant and co-author; Klokotov denies it. Colonel General Leonid Ivashov of the Defence Ministry is also reported to have helped draft it. The book instructs Russia to encourage separatism inside the United States, and it denies that Ukraine can exist.
stops.quote: Ukraine as a state has no geopolitical meaning, no particular cultural import or universal significance, no geographic uniqueness, no ethnic exclusiveness, its certain territorial ambitions represents an enormous danger for all of Eurasia and, without resolving the Ukrainian problem, it is in general senseless to speak about continental politics.
stops.quote_source: Aleksandr Dugin, Osnovy geopolitiki (1997), quoted verbatim on English Wikipedia, 'Foundations of Geopolitics'
suggested_refs: Osnovy geopolitiki: geopoliticheskoe budushchee Rossii (Moscow: Arktogeia, 1997), never authorizedly translated into English

stops.name: Moscow, Fascism: Borderless and Red
stops.date_confidence: the essay and its 1997 date are attested. The attribution of the Ahnenerbe line to this essay specifically is an inference from a shared footnote on English Wikipedia, where the 'intellectual oasis' passage carries the same citation number as the essay's other quoted passage; it is not drawn from reading the essay. Month assigned to order the segment.
stops.campa: He publishes an essay in which the racist and chauvinist aspects of National Socialism are set aside as not what determined the nature of its ideology, and in which the Waffen-SS research institute Ahnenerbe, whose director's name he had borrowed in the cellar, is described as an intellectual oasis. Wolfram Sievers was hanged at Nuremberg for commissioning experiments on prisoners, including the murder of eighty-six Jews for a skeleton collection. Dugin will spend the rest of his career denying that he is a fascist.
stops.quote: an intellectual oasis in the framework of the National Socialist regime
stops.quote_source: Aleksandr Dugin on the Waffen-SS and the Ahnenerbe, quoted on English Wikipedia, 'Aleksandr Dugin', sharing citation [45] with the essay 'Fascism: Borderless and Red' (1997)
suggested_refs: 'Fashizm bezgranichnyy i krasnyy' (1997), the essay Dugin's critics quote most and his defenders explain most

stops.name: State Duma, Okhotny Ryad, adviser to the speaker
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The advisership to Seleznyov and the chairmanship of the geopolitical-expertise section are reported consistently by Dunlop and Laruelle, but no institutional appointment record was independently retrieved. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He is taken on as adviser on geopolitics to Gennady Seleznyov, the communist speaker of the State Duma, and chairs the geopolitical-expertise section of a national-security council attached to the speaker's office. It is the first office of the Russian state the author of Foundations of Geopolitics has ever held. It is not the Kremlin and it is not the cabinet: it is a desk in the parliament building on Okhotny Ryad, with a telephone and a letterhead, three years after 0.85 percent.
suggested_refs: The geopolitical-expertise section of the Duma speaker's security advisory council

segments.name: Eurasia: the Party, the Movement, the Frontier

stops.name: Moscow, the break with Limonov
stops.date_confidence: the 1998 split is attested; the specific quarrel is given in the sources only as an ideological falling-out, and the characterization here of the two men's aims is drawn from their subsequent careers rather than from any statement of theirs. Month assigned to order the segment.
stops.campa: The partnership ends. Limonov wants a street party of young men willing to be arrested; Dugin wants a doctrine installed in ministries and academies. Each accuses the other of having ruined it. Dugin leaves the National Bolsheviks and takes the ideology out with him, leaving Limonov the name, the newspaper and the kids. Limonov will be arrested in 2001 on weapons charges and go to prison. Dugin will be advising the speaker of the Duma and drafting a movement that describes itself as radical centrism.
suggested_refs: Limonov's later account of the split in his own writing

stops.name: Rostov-on-Don, the candidate's dissertation
stops.date_confidence: the degree is attested (ru.wikipedia; MSU ISTINA worker record). Contradiction flagged: the MSU registration record gives 2001 as the award year against a reported 2000 defence, and both figures sit in the same record. The specific dissertation council's building is not documented, so the pin is Rostov-on-Don city centre rather than the university's main building. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: At thirty-eight, three years after writing the book being read in the General Staff, he defends a candidate's dissertation in philosophy at Rostov-on-Don, on the evolution of the paradigmatic foundations of science. The public intellectual precedes the academic by two decades. The credentials arrive afterward and keep arriving: doctor of political sciences, then doctor of sociological sciences in 2011. The records disagree about the year of this first one, giving 2000 for the defence and 2001 for the award, both figures sitting in the same file.
suggested_refs: MSU ISTINA worker record 760705571, which carries both the 2000 and the 2001 date
sources: Russian National Electronic Library dissertation catalogue

stops.name: Moscow, a veterans' club and a new movement
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the founding circumstances; the club is never named in any accessible source beyond 'a veterans' club associated with security and law-enforcement personnel', and no founding-charter document was retrieved. Putin's November 2000 statement is attested; reading it as the trigger is the movement's own account of itself. City-level pin.
stops.campa: In November 2000 Putin says in public that Russia has always perceived itself as a Eurasian country. Dugin reads the sentence as a door and walks through it. He has been in opposition for the whole of his adult life and he is not in opposition now. In April he founds the All-Russian Political Social Movement Eurasia and is elected its leader, on a line of conditional support for the president that he calls radical centrism. The founding is held in a veterans' club full of men from the security and law-enforcement services. No accessible source names the club.
suggested_refs: Putin's November 2000 remark on Russia's Eurasian self-perception

stops.name: Moscow, the party lost and the movement built
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, consistent with the organizational timeline in Wikipedia and Laruelle; no registration or founding document was retrieved for either the 2002 party or the 2003 international movement. The role of Pyotr Suslov is given in secondary profiles only.
stops.campa: Eurasia becomes a registered party in 2002 and then stops being his: the party executive Pyotr Suslov takes the apparatus. Dugin, who has now lost one organization to Limonov and a second to a manager, builds something that cannot be taken away the same way, and never again builds anything that can be voted on or registered away. The International Eurasian Movement has no electoral ambition and no membership roll to capture, only branches, honorary councils, conferences, and correspondents from Ankara to Belgrade to Tehran.
suggested_refs: The International Eurasian Movement and its network of honorary councils

stops.name: Astana, the university named for Gumilyov
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, downgraded from the research pool's attested tag. The honorary professorship is widely reported and institutionally unconfirmed: the university's own article does not mention Dugin at all. The 2004 book is attested. Coordinates from Wikipedia, correcting a 2.4 km error. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: Kazakhstan under Nursultan Nazarbayev is the one post-Soviet state whose president uses the word Eurasia about himself, and it has named a university in Astana for Lev Gumilyov, who invented the term passionarnost and the theory of ethnogenesis that Dugin has been mining for a decade. For the moment the Russian doctrine of a Eurasian union is being written in a Kazakh idiom and addressed to a Kazakh president. Dugin publishes The Eurasian Mission of Nursultan Nazarbayev in 2004 and is named an honorary professor. The university's own account of itself does not mention him anywhere.
suggested_refs: Lev Gumilyov's ethnogenesis and passionarnost, the Soviet-era source of Dugin's Eurasianism
sources: Wikipedia, 'L. N. Gumilyov Eurasian National University'

stops.name: Feodosia, against Sea Breeze
stops.date_confidence: the 2006 anti-NATO protest wave in Crimea and the involvement of Dugin's Eurasian Youth Union are attested; his personal presence at Feodosia specifically, rather than elsewhere in Crimea, is not pinned to a site by any source reviewed. Month assigned to the protest season.
stops.campa: American ships arrive at the Crimean coast for the Sea Breeze exercises and the peninsula will not have them. Dugin's Eurasian Youth Union is in the middle of it, running the young men and the banners, and this is the season in which the Ukrainian security services begin keeping a file on him. For the next eight years the question of who Crimea belongs to is argued by crowds rather than by governments. In Feodosia the protests block the port, the reservists sent ashore to unload are shut into a sanatorium by demonstrators, and the exercises are called off.
suggested_refs: The 2006 Sea Breeze protests at Feodosia and the Eurasian Youth Union's role in them
sources: dossier chronology of the lead-up to the 2007 deportation

stops.name: Simferopol airport, turned around at the border
stops.date_confidence: attested in RFE/RL and Radio Svoboda reporting cited in the dossier; the precise date was not independently re-fetched, because rferl.org returned HTTP 403 on direct fetching. The ban's reported end in 2011 and his reported re-entry by 2012 are secondary reporting only. Administrative measure, not a criminal proceeding.
stops.campa: He lands at Simferopol and is not let through. Ukraine refuses him entry and deports him on the strength of the Eurasian Youth Union's work in Crimea and the anti-NATO protests before it. Seven years after being turned around at this airport he will be arguing in public that the peninsula belongs to Russia, and that the Russian army should come and take a great deal more of the country than the peninsula. The ban is reported to run to 2011, and he is reported able to enter the country again by 2012.
suggested_refs: The Ukrainian entry ban of 2007-2011
sources: RFE/RL, Radio Svoboda (svoboda.org/a/396625.html, cited in dossier)

stops.name: Tskhinvali, five days in August
stops.date_confidence: attested that he travelled to or spoke from South Ossetia during the war and advocated extending Russian power beyond the separatist territories; the exact day of his presence is not fixed by the sources, and the date given is the war's first day. He held no command and gave no orders.
stops.campa: Georgia shells Tskhinvali; Russian columns come south through the Roki tunnel; in five days it is over. Dugin goes to South Ossetia and speaks from it, and what he says is not that Russia should defend the enclave but that Russia should not stop at it, should take Tbilisi, should stop pretending the borders drawn in 1991 mean anything. He is a professor with a microphone standing near a front line, which is the position he will occupy in every war after this one. He holds no command and gives no orders, and the sources do not fix the day he was there.
suggested_refs: The five-day Russo-Georgian war of August 2008

stops.name: Moscow State University, Leninskiye Gory, the Center for Conservative Studies
stops.date_confidence: attested through MSU's own ISTINA course records; the professorship and the acting headship of the Department of Sociology of International Relations from 2009 are attested. The Sociology Faculty's own building is not separately pinned; coordinates mark the main campus. Month assigned to the academic year.
stops.campa: The Faculty of Sociology at Leninskiye Gory gives him a room and students. He lectures on Martin Heidegger and on what he calls postphilosophy: Heidegger, dead since 1976 and never once in Russia, made the central author of a Russian imperial doctrine and taught at the country's chief university to students who will run its ministries. He founds the Center for Conservative Studies with the dean Vladimir Dobrenkov, becomes a professor, and from 2009 acts as head of the Department of Sociology of International Relations.
suggested_refs: MSU ISTINA course records 3521067 and 3521013, the university's own register of what he taught

stops.name: Moscow, The Fourth Political Theory
stops.date_confidence: the 2009 Russian publication and the 2012 Arktos English edition are attested. Month unknown, defaulted. The quotation is from the English translation by Mark Sleboda and Michael Millerman.
stops.campa: The book proposes that the twentieth century offered three political theories, liberalism, communism and fascism, that the first defeated the other two, and that a fourth is needed which is none of them. Its subject is Dasein, taken from Heidegger and made collective: not the individual thrown into the world but the people, the ethnos, the place, the civilization. Arktos Media puts it into English in 2012, translated by Mark Sleboda and Michael Millerman. Almost the whole Anglophone reading of him begins from that edition.
stops.quote: the greatest value of the Fourth Political Theory as a cultural phenomenon; as a community of language, religious belief, daily life, and of sharing resources and efforts; as an organic entity
stops.quote_source: Aleksandr Dugin, The Fourth Political Theory, trans. Mark Sleboda and Michael Millerman (Arktos Media, 2012), quoted on English Wikipedia, 'Fourth Political Theory'
suggested_refs: The Fourth Political Theory (Arktos Media, 2012), the gateway text for Dugin's Anglophone reception

stops.name: Moscow, the Izborsk Club
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for his role: he is one member of more than sixty and does not run the club, which was created under Prokhanov. The club is named for the medieval fortress in Pskov Oblast but operates in Moscow, and the pin marks the operating city, not the namesake town. The date is the date of the quoted Nakanune statement.
stops.campa: Prokhanov gathers more than sixty of them under the name of a medieval fortress in Pskov Oblast: imperialists, communists, Orthodox monarchists, generals, nationalists, men who spent the 1990s despising each other. They meet in Moscow. Dugin is one of them and does not run it. This is the year the Russian state begins to listen to this room rather than to the economists. What he asks for that autumn is not a set of ideas. It is a set of institutions.
stops.quote: We want patriotic radio, TV, patriotic experts, patriotic clubs. We want the media that expresses national interests.
stops.quote_source: Aleksandr Dugin, statement on Nakanune.ru, 28 September 2012, quoted in English on English Wikipedia, 'Aleksandr Dugin'
suggested_refs: The Izborsk Club and its journal, the meeting point of the Russian imperial right after 2012
sources: Juliette Faure, European Journal of International Security (Cambridge)
Laruelle on the Izborsk Club, JSTOR 43919640

stops.name: Sevastopol, Crimea and what is not enough
stops.date_confidence: attested that he supported the annexation and advocated a far larger Novorossiya project, and that he was in contact with separatist figures. His own itinerary within Crimea in March 2014 is not itemized in any source reviewed; the pin marks Sevastopol as the symbolic centre of the annexation, not a documented location of his. The date is the date of the annexation treaty.
stops.campa: Russian troops without insignia take the peninsula, a referendum is held under their guns, and the annexation goes through in three weeks. Dugin supports it and says at once that it is not enough: what is required is Novorossiya, the whole southern and eastern arc of Ukraine from Kharkiv to Odesa. He is on the telephone to separatist commanders and in public demanding open Russian intervention. The Kremlin takes Crimea and stops there. He does not stop, and within three months it costs him his chair.
suggested_refs: The Novorossiya project of 2014, advocated far beyond what the Russian state was then prepared to do

stops.name: Moscow State University, the order cancelled
stops.date_confidence: attested, and contested in real time: Rector Sadovnichy cancelled an order that would have reappointed him through 2019, MSU's press service denied he had been fired, and his existing fixed-term contract then lapsed later in the year. All three statements are true of the same summer and the sources are reported here as disagreeing about the mechanism, not about the outcome.
stops.campa: On the second of May dozens of people burn to death in the trade union building in Odesa. Dugin's public remarks about killing, made in connection with that day, produce a petition against him. Rector Viktor Sadovnichy cancels the order that would have reappointed him to 2019. The university's press service denies that he has been fired. His existing contract simply runs out later in the year and is not renewed. He is fifty-two and has no university post, and the three accounts of how he lost it are all true of the same summer.
suggested_refs: RBC and Novaya Gazeta reporting of 27 and 28 June 2014, which disagree with the MSU press service

stops.name: Moscow, the designation arrives
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the primary document: the OFAC page (ofac.treasury.gov/recent-actions/20150311) timed out on direct fetch, so the designation rests on Wikipedia's relay of the Treasury action. The stop is pinned at Moscow, where he is, rather than at Washington, where the paper was signed. 'Putin's brain' is a label whose accuracy the same sources dispute.
stops.campa: The United States Treasury adds him to the Ukraine-related sanctions list under Executive Order 13660, naming his leadership of the Eurasian Youth Union and stating that the organization recruited fighters for the self-proclaimed Donetsk People's Republic. His assets in American jurisdiction are blocked and Americans may not deal with him. He is in Moscow when it happens and it changes nothing about his day. Abroad, the label attaching to him in these years is Putin's brain; those who know the Kremlin say his influence has been greatly exaggerated.
suggested_refs: The OFAC designation of 11 March 2015 under Executive Order 13660
sources: US Treasury sanctions action, 11 March 2015 (page not reachable on direct fetch)

stops.name: Moscow, Tsargrad
stops.date_confidence: date contradiction flagged and not resolved: ru.wikipedia dates his chief editorship to 2016-2017, while the channel launched in 2015 and several Western profiles date his appointment from the launch. Month unknown, defaulted. No credible source makes Dugin an owner of Tsargrad; Malofeev is the owner. Studio address not documented.
stops.campa: Konstantin Malofeev, an Orthodox monarchist financier, launches a television channel and calls it Tsargrad, the old Slavic name for Constantinople, and Dugin becomes its chief editor. He is not an owner and never was. The tenure is short, and the sources cannot agree on when it ran: ru.wikipedia dates it 2016 to 2017, other accounts from the channel's launch in 2015. The association outlasts the job. After thirty years of trying to get his doctrine inside an institution, the institution turns out to be a broadcast studio funded by one man: the Katehon network, the Tsargrad Institute, the streams, the translations into eight languages.
suggested_refs: Tsargrad TV and the Katehon network, both funded by Konstantin Malofeev

stops.name: Rome, the Traditionalist and the strategist
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the meeting is known from Benjamin Teitelbaum's War for Eternity, based on his interviews with both men, and no independent record was reached. City-level pin, no venue in the sourcing. Month unknown, defaulted.

Both men have read Guenon and Evola and believe the modern West is in the last phase of a cycle rather than in a bad decade. Both want the populist revolt to be about something older than tax rates. They disagree about Russia, about China, and about Iran, which is most of the distance between an American nationalism and a Eurasian one. The account comes from a scholar who interviewed them both, and there is no independent record of the meeting.

stops.name: Amsterdam, against Bernard-Henri Levy
stops.date_confidence: attested for September 2019; the specific hall is not documented in the sources reviewed and the pin is city-level. Day of month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: Bernard-Henri Levy comes to Amsterdam to debate him and the evening is staged as the Enlightenment against its enemy. Levy defends universal human rights and the individual person. Dugin argues that the universal is one civilization's particular, dressed as a law of nature and exported at gunpoint, and that there is no single humanity, only peoples. Neither convinces the other and neither is meant to. A Dutch audience has bought tickets to look at the Russian the newspapers call Putin's brain, and he is plainly enjoying himself.

stops.name: Moscow, Noomakhia closed at twenty-four volumes
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the completion of the series with the three-volume Russian Logos rests on publisher-catalogue claims cited in the source crawl, and no publisher page was re-fetched directly. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He closes Noomakhia, Wars of the Mind, with the last three volumes of the Russian Logos. Twenty-four volumes, one civilization at a time, each read through three Logoi: Apollo, vertical and luminous; Dionysus, mediating between above and below; Cybele, chthonic and maternal, which is where he puts the modern West. The argument of the whole thing is that every civilization thinks in its own way and owes none of the others an explanation. It is the largest structure he has built. Nobody has read all of it.

He has been writing toward this week since the wooden barrack on Yuzhinsky Pereulok, and the state now doing it does not quote him and does not acknowledge that he exists.

stops.name: Mozhayskoye Highway, the car
stops.date_confidence: attested; coordinates and the approximate time of 21:45 from Wikipedia, 'Darya Dugina', correcting two mutually inconsistent and both incorrect pins in the research pool. Responsibility is contested at four separate evidentiary levels and none of them is a court finding as to who placed the device. The Washington Post reported that some US officials suspected Aleksandr Dugin was the intended target, albeit with Darya Dugina also being in the car.
stops.campa: At about a quarter to ten in the evening, on the Mozhayskoye Highway, a device attached beneath the Land Cruiser detonates. The car burns. Darya Dugina dies at the scene, aged twenty-nine. Her father, driving home by another route, is brought to the roadside and is filmed there with his hands at his head, looking at the wreck. Russia's FSB names a Ukrainian citizen. A Tula court will later convict two men of forging a vehicle registration document and of nothing else. No court has named who placed the bomb.

stops.name: Moscow, the Order of Courage

The Russian text of the statement no longer resolves at its source; what survives is a translation of it.

stops.name: Russian State University for the Humanities, the school named for Ilyin

stops.name: Russian State University for the Humanities, RGGU Against Ilyin
stops.date_confidence: attested through Meduza's feature, which is the only source reached for the petition and the Student Anti-Fascist Front; the RSUH article does not mention Dugin or the petition at all.
stops.campa: A student petition titled RGGU Against Ilyin goes up on the twelfth of April, objecting to the name over the door and to the man appointed behind it. It spreads to other universities within weeks and becomes the Student Anti-Fascist Front, the first organized campus opposition inside Russia since the invasion began. In a country where a placard can bring fifteen years, the signatories put their names to it and risk expulsion, conscription and prosecution. What they are objecting to is the naming of a school of politics.
